newsitem.title: USA: US SEC chief warns against hasty litigation reform.
newsitem.headline: US SEC chief warns against hasty litigation reform.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt told lawmakers Thursday not to move too quickly on reforms that would restrict certain securities class actions from making their way into court, including state courts.

"I do not oppose reform -- only reform that is too sweeping and reform that is too hasty. Let us not replace the race to the courthouse with a race to the Capitol," Levitt told the Senate Banking Committee's securities subcommittee.

In a letter released at the hearing, President Clinton said he is monitoring the situation and that his economic advisers will soon provide him with recommendations as to whether or not even further reforms are needed.

"As we work through this process, we should be guided by the same principles that were applicable to the Reform Act debate: a strong stand against abuse of the legal system, whether in federal or state court, in the bringing and settling of actions," Clinton wrote in the July 23 letter to Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee.

The hearing came as leaders from the technology industry, venture capitalists and the securities industry have been pushing Congress for more reforms to keep what they call frivolous lawsuits from making their way to court, including state courts.

In 1995, Congress enacted reforms over a presidential veto that aim to restrict such suits, but many industry representatives say litigators have gotten around those reforms by taking cases to state courts.
Despite the administration's concerns about moving too quickly, lawmakers on the panel are likely to move ahead with more reforms, to mirror the effort underway by some House lawmakers.
"We clearly did not do enough and I'm concerned about it," said Senator Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican and chair of the subcommittee. Dodd raised the same concerns.

"While the number of federal filings doesn't greatly concern me, I am deeply concerned over the increase in state court filings," Dodd said. "My fear is that the state court filings represent those suits that aren't strong enough to stand up in federal court."
